Testo del commento:
It's definitely a personal pet peeve, but I can't stand stories that mechanize the human body to personify the processes within it. Especially the human brain, because I (too) like to study psychology and biological psychological science. To me, it feels like it flattens the real wonder and science behind the very cool things happening in our bodies that fuel us and puts it in a pointlessly suburban and unnatural context. It doesn't feel creative to me, it just feels lazy, because the science is never really accurate or good. You can't say you're enticing your children to learn more when they get inspired by something that is factually incorrect. I get that films aren't trying to be textbooks or primarily educational, or whatever, it's a taste thing, but it's just foundationally against my own tastes and weirdly has been since I was a child.

I don't mind humans shrunk down to explore the human body stories though. Cells at Work : NO. Innerspace : YES.
Discussione / regola applicata: Critica la rappresentazione del corpo umano perché scientificamente inaccurata e poco creativa. Esprime gusti personali, ma non chiarisce se il valore della propria visione risieda nell’apprendimento o nell’esperienza vissuta. Il riferimento all’educazione dei bambini riguarda una giustificazione che contesta: non basta per assegnare strumentale.

also, regarding he real T.E. Lawrence, I think that discussion is not really that relevant in this case, because that was a different man, and the Lawrence in the film is a different man.

Testo del commento:
You wouldn’t call *Saving Private Ryan* a “heroic blockbuster?” Do you object to both descriptors or only in combination? It’s a popcorn flick for people to feel self-serious at. It’s *Titanic* “for men/adults.”

It’s technically proficient. I’m not calling it bad. At all. (Ditto *Titanic.* Or *Avatar*, whose plot points are equally as serious.) But it was an absolute blockbuster, and it paints things in a heroic light. (“Mellish didn’t even know what his sacrifice was for, but ‘Ours is not to reason why…’”)

It doesn’t use the same paint-by-numbers tropes directors have employed since the three hour period piece costume drama went out of vogue in the 1960s. That’s why it’s modern / “so sophisticated.”

It doesn’t have anything new or notable or controversial to say about war in general or WW2 in particular. However it did say what it did have to say to a mass release audience in time for special edition DVDs to be paired with Tom Brokaw’s book.

I think *Lincoln* is a stellar comp for *Saving Private Ryan* in terms of middlebrow folk history based on a kernel of truth. I don’t say any of this because I hate or dislike either, but we should not give ourselves over to historical epics to the extent they become our only sources of information about the past, and I would have to do that to find either profound.
Discussione / regola applicata: Analizza eroismo, storia e mercato di Saving Private Ryan; non racconta un proprio vissuto estetico. Il monito sulle fonti storiche non basta a renderlo strumentale.

Testo del commento:
I think the best place to look to will be books. A few suggestions with the caveat that I'm not sure if they are exactly what you're looking for:

* *Japanese Film and the Challenge of Video*, Tom Mes (quite new still so a bit pricey)
   * This book champions V-Cinema, why it's been overlooked, and why it shouldn't be.
* *Contemporary Japanese Film*, Mark Schilling
   * A majority of this book is profiles on/interviews with various directors that you may love, but the beginning has some good insights that I think may be what you are looking for.
* *The Midnight Eye Guide to New Japanese Film*, Tom Mes and Jasper Sharp
   * As with *Contemporary Japanese Film*, this book is largely profiles on directors and a selection of their films. This may be worth looking into if enough of the covered directors are of interest to you.

There is a great making-of on the *Tampopo* Blu-ray released by Criterion, it's feature length and made by Juzo Itami himself. This is, of course, not a 90s film but I did find it to be fascinating since he covers almost every aspect of making this film and it's extra useful since he is the director and not a 3rd party observer.
Discussione / regola applicata: Consiglia libri e un making-of come fonti per conoscere il cinema giapponese e la realizzazione di un film. Il making-of è apprezzato esplicitamente per le informazioni offerte dal regista. Si applica la regola 1.1 sulle raccomandazioni di studio e approfondimento: le opere consigliate sono mezzi per acquisire conoscenze. L’aggettivo “affascinante” non sposta il criterio prevalente.

Testo del commento:
Sure, you've got a great starting point there, wanting to learn more about films spanning various genres, periods, and cultures. The key is immersion, watching as many films as you can and not just watching, but actively engaging - What did you see? What did it make you feel? Part of the fun is finding connections, spotting common themes or visual ideas between different films or directors. 

As for educational resources, you might consider auditing film studies courses online. Websites like Coursera and EdX offer free and paid courses from universities around the world. For example, I know that Yale has a course on Film History available on Coursera. Check out Kanopy as well; many public libraries subscribe to it and it offers a vast array of classic, international, and indie films. 

However, remember that no course will make you a film expert; the true appreciation of cinema comes with time, patience and personal reflection. Start by watching, researching, and reflecting on films. With time, your personal taste, critical eye, and understanding of cinema will naturally develop. Happy viewing!
Discussione / regola applicata: Propone visioni, corsi, ricerca e riflessione come percorso per sviluppare conoscenza cinematografica e capacità critica. Regola 1.1 sui consigli di studio: il fine formativo organizza l'intero consiglio.

Their point is this:

While No Country for Old Men is ostensibly a western, it is far enough removed from the bulk of the genre to be anomalous.  The change in time period brings with it considerable changes: the aesthetic, tone, and general tropes are far different from that of the majority of westerns such that comparisons aren’t really useful.  The cheeseburger analogy is because a cheeseburger is technically a sandwich, but few people consider it one because of all the differences it has to the bulk of what we think of when we think of sandwiches.  If someone asked someone ‘what’s your favorite sandwich’ and you responded ‘cheeseburger’, most people would find that sort of response to not be what they were looking for, even if you really did like cheeseburgers more than any sandwich.  It’s the same with Old Country for No Men: no matter how good it might be, it lacks enough of the most prevalent features of westerns for that poster to feel like it belongs in the conversation of ‘best westerns’.

I don’t necessarily agree but I thought I’d explain what they meant.
Discussione / regola applicata: Spiega perché un altro utente escluda No Country for Old Men dal confronto tra western, discutendo convenzioni di genere e analogie. Non descrive il valore della propria esperienza di visione. Inoltre, precisa di non condividere necessariamente la posizione spiegata: non possiamo attribuirgliela come framing personale.

Testo del commento:
> As a psychologist, I can confidently say there are many psychology-related mistakes that movies make.

As a chemist, I have never seen a single movie portray a real life lab routine or work accurately. However, that doesn't make them flawed or insufficient because for all the intents, the purpose of those scenes aren't to educate but to convey a specific meaning or elicit an emotion to the scene/viewer.

Walter White mixing stuff in his trailer isn't an accurate portrayal of how to cook meth, but for all intents and purposes the scenes are perfect because they get the point (the protagonist using his professional chemical knowledge to synthesize drugs in haphazard and dangerous situations) across.

Same for psychology in movies. Watching a genius Russel Crowe write equations on windows because he's schizophrenic and somehow this makes him brilliant is completely bogus, but it serves as a plot point the same way any protagonist who ever mixed unnamed magic powders to make a super efficient explosive in order to escape from their captors or something.
Discussione / regola applicata: Discute la funzione narrativa delle inesattezze scientifiche e psicologiche. Il richiamo a suscitare emozioni è una teoria sulle scene, non un valore della propria esperienza esplicitato.

These films are part of the canon of world cinema for a reason; they elevated movie making to an art form by revolutionizing the way films were made or how stories were told on screen, they changed the way people thought about cinema.
